title: Two number systems
goal: Master the biggest stumbling block for foreign learners: Korean has two sets of numbers that cannot stand in for each other. Count things, give your age, and read prices.
bekal: say the native Korean numbers from one to twenty
say the Sino-Korean numbers and read prices
choose the right set depending on what is being counted
use the counters 개, 명, 잔, 병, 살
ask how many with 몇 and how much with 얼마

dialogs.title: 대화 — At the convenience store by campus
dialogs.intro: Ani is buying a few things. Listen closely: in this one short conversation both number systems are used side by side, and they never get mixed up.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Hello. Two bottles of water, please.

lines.speaker: 점원:
lines.id: Sure, here you go. Do you need anything else?
lines.literal: yes, here — is. more — needed — thing — exists (honorific)?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: One coffee and three pieces of bread, please.
lines.literal: coffee — one — cup — and — bread — three — item — give.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Here you are. Oh, by the way, how much is that bread over there?
lines.literal: here — is. ah, by-the-way, that-over-there — bread — as-for — how-much — is?

lines.speaker: 점원:
lines.id: That one is fifteen hundred won. It's a bit pricey.
lines.literal: that — as-for — one-thousand-five-hundred — won — is. a-little — expensive.

lines.speaker: 점원:
lines.id: Sure. Are you a student? There's a student discount.
lines.literal: yes. student — are (honorific)? student — discount — that — exists.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. Thank you!

lines.speaker: 점원:
lines.id: That's nine thousand won altogether. Have a good day.
lines.literal: all — nine-thousand — won — is. in-peace — go.

notes: **The two number systems are not a matter of style.** 물 두 병 uses native Korean numbers because bottles are being counted; 팔천 원 uses Sino-Korean numbers because money is read as a figure. Swapping them doesn't just sound odd — often it isn't understood at all.

**The order is noun + number + counter.** 커피 한 잔, not 한 잔 커피. That's the reverse of English ("one cup of coffee"), so drill it consciously until it's automatic. If you flip it, Koreans will understand — but you'll sound like you're translating in your head.
**The first four numbers change shape before a counter.** 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네. Plus 스물→스무. All others stay the same. Memorize these five, because they're the numbers you'll use most.
**하나 on its own can be used without a counter.** 하나 주세요 = "one, please" — correct and very common when the item is obvious. But as soon as a counter appears, it must become 한: 한 개 주세요.

**어서 오세요 is not an ordinary greeting.** Shopkeepers say it to customers, never the other way round. You'll never say it unless you own the shop. A simple 안녕하세요 is enough in reply, or just say what you want.
**주세요 is the most useful word in this whole unit.** Literally "please give", it ends almost every request for something: 물 주세요, 계산서 주세요, 이거 주세요. The dictionary form is 주다 (to give).

**좀 softens whatever is around it.** Literally "a little" (from 조금), its main job is to cushion. 비싸요 = expensive (sounds like a complaint). 좀 비싸요 = a bit pricey (sounds like a polite remark). Slip in 좀 and your whole sentence sounds friendlier.

**학생이세요? uses the honorific 시.** The clerk is showing respect to a customer, so she doesn't say 학생이에요? but 학생이세요?. You don't need to use it yet — just recognize it, because you'll hear it in every shop in Korea.

grammars.title: Native Korean numbers
body: Used for **counting**: numbers of things, numbers of people, age, and hours. They stop at 99, and in practice are rarely used above 40.
after: Eleven to nineteen are formed by putting 열 in front: 열하나, 열둘, 열셋 … 열아홉. Twenty-one = 스물하나. Same pattern as English "twenty-one".
여덟 (eight) is written with two final consonants but read *yeodeol* — the ㅂ is completely silent unless a vowel particle follows.

grammars.title: Sino-Korean numbers
body: Used for **reading figures**: money, minutes, dates, phone numbers, addresses, measurements. This is the only system that can climb into the millions.
after: **Korean counts large numbers in units of ten thousand, not a thousand.** 만 = 10,000. A hundred thousand isn't a new word but "ten 만" = 십만. One million = "a hundred 만" = 백만. It feels strange at first and matters a lot in Korea, because everyday prices sit right in that range.
⚠️ **일 is not said before 백, 천 and 만.** A hundred is 백, not 일백. A thousand is 천, not 일천. Ten thousand is likewise just **만**, and a hundred million has its own word: 억.
Prices in the dialogue: 팔천 원 = 8,000 won, 천오백 원 = 1,500 won, 구천 원 = 9,000 won. Note there are no spaces inside the number, and 원 stands apart.

grammars.title: The most common counters
body: Korean can't count nouns directly — there's always a counter between the number and the noun, like "two **cups** of coffee" or "three **sheets** of paper" in English, but for everything.

after: ⚠️ **분 has two meanings that use different number systems.** 세 **분** (three people, honorific) uses native Korean numbers; 삼십 **분** (thirty minutes) uses Sino-Korean. The number system itself tells you which meaning is intended.
If you really forget the counter, **개 is almost always acceptable** for objects. It isn't always the best fit, but it never leaves you misunderstood.

sections.title: Age, and why people ask about it so often

blocks.text: The question 몇 살이에요? ("how old are you?") comes much earlier in a Korean introduction than English speakers are used to. It isn't nosiness: age decides the speech style both sides use, what they call each other, and who pays for lunch. Without knowing it, a Korean doesn't know how to talk to you.
There is a different honorific form you'll hear from older people: 연세가 어떻게 되세요? The answer stays the same.

blocks.title: Terms of address that depend on age
items: Women call an older man **오빠**; men call an older man **형**.
Women call an older woman **언니**; men call an older woman **누나**.
Someone younger is a **동생** (or just called by name). People the same age use name + 씨 until you both agree to go casual.
⚠️ Those first four terms are for people you're **close** to, not for anyone older. Calling the convenience-store cashier 오빠 isn't polite — it's out of place.
